Proving the product of two primitive polynomials in a UFD R[x] is primitive involves understanding the definitions of primitive polynomials and the properties of UFDs.

In a Unique Factorization Domain (UFD) R[x], a polynomial f(x) is primitive if its content (the greatest common divisor of its coefficients) is 1. This means that the coefficients of f(x) have no common factors other than units (elements with multiplicative inverse).

Now, let f(x) and g(x) be two primitive polynomials in R[x]. We want to show that their product f(x)g(x) is also primitive.

Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that f(x)g(x) is not primitive. Then, there exists a unit u in R such that u divides all the coefficients of f(x)g(x). Since u is a unit, it has a multiplicative inverse v in R.

Consider the polynomials f(x) and g(x) modulo u. Since u divides all the coefficients of f(x)g(x), we have f(x)g(x) ≡ 0 (mod u). This implies that either f(x) ≡ 0 (mod u) or g(x) ≡ 0 (mod u).

Since f(x) and g(x) are primitive, their contents are 1. Therefore, u cannot divide all the coefficients of f(x) or g(x), which means that either f(x) ≡ 0 (mod u) or g(x) ≡ 0 (mod u) is impossible.

This contradiction shows that our assumption that f(x)g(x) is not primitive is false. Therefore, the product of two primitive polynomials in a UFD R[x] is indeed primitive.

Now, let's consider the second part of the problem. Suppose f(x) and g(x) are coprime in R[x]. We want to show that they are also coprime in F[x], the field of fractions.

In F[x], the polynomials f(x) and g(x) are coprime if and only if their greatest common divisor (GCD) is 1. Since f(x) and g(x) are coprime in R[x], their GCD in R[x] is 1.

We need to show that their GCD in F[x] is also 1. Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that the GCD of f(x) and g(x) in F[x] is not 1.

Then, there exists a non-unit element a in R such that a divides all the coefficients of the GCD of f(x) and g(x) in F[x]. Since a is a non-unit, it has a multiplicative inverse b in R.

Consider the polynomials f(x) and g(x) modulo a. Since a divides all the coefficients of the GCD of f(x) and g(x) in F[x], we have f(x)g(x) ≡ 0 (mod a). This implies that either f(x) ≡ 0 (mod a) or g(x) ≡ 0 (mod a).

Since f(x) and g(x) are coprime in R[x], their GCD in R[x] is 1. Therefore, a cannot divide all the coefficients of f(x) or g(x), which means that either f(x) ≡ 0 (mod a) or g(x) ≡ 0 (mod a) is impossible.

This contradiction shows that our assumption that the GCD of f(x) and g(x) in F[x] is not 1 is false. Therefore, the polynomials f(x) and g(x) are indeed coprime in F[x].
